doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Playing second trumpet in his father's polka band, and polka links to jazz
summary: He sat with his father's Austro-Hungarian polka band at picnics, and sees polka as close to two-beat jazz, as in Germany, and in Ken Peplowski's background.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yeah. I think it just became a natural thing and he played in a polka band, he had come over from Austria-Hungry, so I’m really first generation American. And every Sunday during the summer months he would be playing with a polka band at picnics and stuff, and I would sit alongside him and play second and third trumpet in the polka band. I don’t think it was anybody’s intent that I would get into music full time. Even then, economically it was a struggle kind of a thing to consider that. But I think they always wanted music as a part of my life. And we always had music around the house.
Did they play polka music in the house on records?
Not really, not too much of it, no. My father would bring home a whole smattering of trumpet players, Harry James, you know the things that he was doing, and trumpet players in general.
When you were sitting by him in the polka bands, was it written music?

Yes, it was all written. A lot of triple time [scats]. Very similar really to two beat jazz. In fact it’s one of the things that I notice when I play in Germany. I think one of the reasons — my theory on one of the reasons that Germans love this red hot jazz, and they really love traditional jazz, it’s very similar to the polka. I mean [scats]. And if you go out to the west coast and hear the Turk Murphy offshoots, the 50 or so bands that are out there, it’s banjo and tuba, and it’s two-beat [scats]. And you can polka to that whole thing. And I think it’s why a lot of the older people do like this two-beat music, they can walk to it, they walk on one and three, as opposed to clapping on two and four.
That’s a great point. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

I think there’s quite a bit of validity in that. It makes it easy for some people to dance to, one and three. They can walk, they can parade, they can carry their umbrellas like New Orleans. So anyway.

So anyway, Ken Peplowski, who I work with a lot, also played for a polka band out in the Cleveland, Ohio area. He cut his chops, got going with that fast clarinet playing from playing polkas. That’s what got him into it anyway.
It serves you well I think, technique-wise at least.
